results.content:
The pitch is compelling. The reality involves a steep learning curve. Most users spend their first two weeks watching their agent burn through API credits while looping on the same task eight times in a row. The gap between the demo screenshots and daily reliable use is real.

This guide distills seven operational principles that consistently separate stable OpenClaw deployments from frustrated abandonments. They come from community-tested patterns, not theory.

## 1. Use Tiered Model Routing — Stop Feeding Everything to Your Best Model [...] ## Get Ewan Mak’s stories in your inbox

Join Medium for free to get updates from this writer.

This aligns with a core principle in AI agent system design — an agent’s effectiveness scales with the structured knowledge it can access.

Press enter or click to view image in full size

## 6. Model Quality Determines Agent Quality

Much of the frustration users attribute to OpenClaw actually stems from underlying model limitations in tool-calling reliability. Chat quality and agent quality are different problems. A model that produces fluent conversational responses may still fail at reliably invoking tools, parsing returns, and chaining multi-step operations.

Based on community feedback, here’s how current models perform in agent contexts:

Press enter or click to view image in full size [...] ## 5. Persist What Works in Workspace Files

OpenClaw’s compaction mechanism (context compression) gradually loses important context over extended use. If your agent has to relearn your preferences and past decisions every time it starts a new session, performance degrades steadily.

The practical fix: maintain your workspace’s core documentation files. `USER.md` stores your personal information and preferences. `AGENTS.md` defines agent roles and behavioral guidelines. `HEARTBEAT.md`configures scheduled check-in timing and content. `MEMORY.md` holds long-term memory and key decision records. Writing critical decisions and successful configurations into these files dramatically reduces the agent's re-learning overhead.

results.title: Why OpenClaw’s Crisis Is Everyone’s Problem
results.content:
OpenClaw is specific. The problem is not.

Every agentic framework that achieves viral consumer adoption before enterprise governance frameworks exist will follow this arc. The tool will be useful. Employees will install it. It will accumulate credentials. Corporate IT will discover exposure after the fact. The ban will come too late. The governance infrastructure will be assembled reactively, incompletely, under pressure.

The question is whether the industry learns from the first documented case or treats it as an OpenClaw-specific failure and waits for the next one. [...] Audit trails that capture agent reasoning, not just actions. What an agent did is less useful than why it decided to do it. Post-incident analysis of the Yue case required reconstructing the compaction event from indirect evidence. Enterprise incident response for agent failures needs session-level reasoning logs what context was present, what was compressed, and what instruction state existed at the point of action.

## The Bottom Line

OpenClaw was built in an hour for personal use. Its security documentation explicitly says it is not designed for enterprise deployment. It ended up running on 135,000 exposed machines, accumulating credentials to corporate infrastructure across thousands of organizations, before any governance framework existed to evaluate whether it should be there. [...] The answer depends on whether enterprises treat OpenClaw as an anomaly, one scrappy open-source tool with bad defaults and poor security hygiene, or as a preview. The defaults were bad. The security hygiene was poor. And the pattern will repeat with every agentic tool that follows, because the pattern is not about the tool. It is about the governance category that doesn’t exist yet.

Software that acts autonomously on behalf of humans, with persistent credentials and machine-speed execution, is not a chatbot. It is not an application. It is not a service account. It is a new class of privileged actor in enterprise environments, and every existing framework, IAM, endpoint security, software procurement, and compliance was built before it existed.
